role_tag_en: teacher of ritual and humaneness; founder of the Ru tradition
dating_basis: Death: Zuozhuan Ai 16 (contemporary annal). Birth: Gongyang/Guliang give Xiang 21 (-552), Shiji gives -551.
short_bio_en: Minor official in Lu who became the most influential teacher in Chinese history; his sayings were compiled by disciples as the Analects.

role_tag_en: traditional author of the Daodejing
dating_basis: Shiji 63 already records three conflicting identifications; the text bearing his name is datable to c. 400-250 (Guodian slips c. 300). Person may be a construct.
short_bio_en: Traditionally an archivist at the Zhou court whom Confucius consulted; the historical person is uncertain, the text is not.

role_tag_en: Confucian; theorist of innate human goodness and the people's right to depose tyrants
dating_basis: Floruit from named rulers he addressed (King Hui of Liang, King Xuan of Qi); exact years disputed. SLICE (added 2026-10-04, Sophia r9-1): the whole life range lies after the 600-400 BCE pilot slice; until 2026-10-04 that held this row to a lineage endpoint (is_protagonist=0, no events; D-08). D-20 lifts the slice and D-08's endpoint restriction for the China pillar only (R_CN ranges over 800-200), so the row is now a protagonist at the range its sources support, unchanged. He has no event row yet, so the map home shows him in the tray (no event gives him a place) until a Phase B event lands. PHASE B, 2026-10-04 (Sophia r9-4): the sentence above saying he has no event row no longer holds. E_CN_055 (Mencius comes to King Hui of Liang, -336 on Shiji 15's chronology, at PL_DALIANG, presence 'present') is his first event row, and the map home's count rule now draws him at Daliang (no override). The birth and death ranges above are unchanged and were NOT re-read this session: Shiji 74, read this session (zh.wikisource.org page 史記/卷074 (revision 7908177, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session)), gives no year for either, only the order of his travels (孟軻，騶人也。受業子思之門人。道既通，游事齊宣王，宣王不能用。適梁，梁惠王不果所言，則見以為迂遠而闊於事情。).
short_bio_en: Second sage of the Ru tradition; argued human nature is good and that Heaven's mandate is read in the people's acceptance.

role_tag_en: founder of Buddhism; teacher of the Middle Way
dating_basis: Short chronology (death c. 400 +/-20) per Bechert 1991-97 and Gombrich; traditional Theravada date -543, older Western consensus -483/-486.
short_bio_en: Prince turned wandering ascetic who taught a path between indulgence and self-mortification across the Gangetic kingdoms.

role_tag_en: 24th Jain tirthankara; teacher of non-violence
dating_basis: DEATH, derived from the corpus's own evidence (E_IN_015): MN 104:2.1 and DN 29:1.3 both report that the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan had recently passed away at Pāvā, as news brought to the Buddha while he is alive and teaching (dn29:2.1-2.6), and DN 29:14.4 has the Buddha call himself, in that same discourse, advanced in years and in the final stage of life, which places the report late in his teaching life but gives no year. The death therefore falls inside the Buddha's teaching life and before his own death; on the short chronology adopted for P_BUDDHA (Bechert) that is the corpus's teaching-life frame, -471/-380 (the earliest going forth, birth -500 plus 29, to the latest death), and the range is that frame and no narrower. mn104:2.1-2.5, dn29:1.1-2.7 and dn29:14.4 read at their locators on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in suttacentral/bilara-data, published branch, Sujato's translation; dn2:7.2, read the same day, has a minister describe the same teacher as advanced in years and in the final stage of life in Ajatasattu's reign. The death range -470/-425 this row carried before followed a scholarly position it did not name and touched E_IN_015 at one year only; it is replaced. The Jain traditional date (death -527) lies OUTSIDE this range and is recorded, not adopted; no Jain source was read. BIRTH -540/-500 still follows the unnamed scholarly position that ties Mahavira to the Buddha's generation as an older contemporary; no source for it was read, and it is the row's weakest cell. OPEN: the lead may prefer a range spanning both chronologies; that needs the Jain traditional birth date verified against a citable edition.
short_bio_en: Contemporary and rival of the Buddha; systematised ahimsa and asceticism as the Jain path.

role_tag_en: priest-prophet of the Babylonian exile
dating_basis: Dated oracles in the book run 593-571; person known only from the book bearing his name.
short_bio_en: Deported to Babylonia in 597; his visions reframed God as present outside the land and each person as responsible for their own guilt.

role_tag_en: anonymous exilic poet-prophet; author of Isaiah 40-55
dating_basis: Author unknown; text dated by its references to Cyrus (Isa 44:28, 45:1) to c. 545-538. wikidata_qid Q1201710 added under ruling L-25: the item's description reads 'anonymous author of chapters 40-55 of the Book of Isaiah, writing during the Babylonian Exile' (read by the site owner at wikidata.org, 2026-09-07/08, relayed by the lead) - it models the PERSON, which is exactly what this row models, so conventions §1 ('fill it whenever the entity has a Wikidata item') applies. The earlier ruling that this cell stay blank rested on the premise that no author item exists; that premise was wrong. historicity stays 'anonymous': the item is the hypothesised author, not a named person. The text of Isaiah 40-55 has no item of its own (see W_ISAIAH_40_55). NOTE: people.csv has no 'note' column, so this provenance lives here.
short_bio_en: The unnamed author of Isaiah 40-55, whose poems declare a single God of all nations and name Cyrus as his instrument.

role_tag_en: founder of the Achaemenid empire
dating_basis: Nabonidus Chronicle, Cyrus Cylinder, Herodotus 1. Birth year inferred. The bio's 'including the Judeans' rests on Ezra 1 (E_IL_004; Q_063 quotes 1:2-3), read 2026-10-13 in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (licence 'Public Domain' read off the response): Cyrus's proclamation that whoever is among 'all His people' may 'go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah' (1:3), and at 1:11 'they of the captivity were brought up from Babylon unto Jerusalem'. The Cyrus Cylinder names no Judah, as Q_098's note records.
short_bio_en: Persian king who took Media, Lydia and Babylon within twenty years and let deported peoples, including the Judeans, return home.

role_tag_en: Achaemenid king; author of the Behistun inscription
dating_basis: Death -486 is fixed by dated Babylonian tablets: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 14 (read 2026-10-13) list the last tablets of his year 36 from September to November 486 (the latest, 7 November, with a damaged day numeral) and Xerxes recognised by 1 December 486, and conclude that Darius died in November 486. (Until 2026-10-13 this sentence also named the Behistun inscription, which was carved c. 520-518 (E_PE_003) and cannot date his death.) Birth is not attested anywhere: Herodotus 1.209 makes Darius son of Hystaspes about twenty years old (ἐὼν τότε ἡλικίην ἐς εἴκοσί κου μάλιστα ἔτεα) at Cyrus's crossing of the Araxes, c. 530/529, so a birth c. 550 is a modern back-calculation; the range -553/-547 records that inference, not a source. Herodotus 3 narrates 522 and gives no birth year.
short_bio_en: Seized the throne in 522 and justified it in a long account in his own voice carved at Behistun, framed as truth against the Lie.

role_tag_en: prophet of Ahura Mazda; author of the Gathas (traditional)
dating_basis: Linguistic dating of the Gathas c. 1200-1000 (Boyce, Skjaervo) vs Sasanian tradition '258 years before Alexander' (c. 588). Range deliberately wide.
short_bio_en: Composer of the Gathas, hymns that cast the cosmos as a contest between truth and the lie and the individual as a chooser between them.

role_tag_en: Athenian lawgiver and poet
dating_basis: Archonship 594/3 from the archon list (Aristotle Ath. Pol. 5-12; Plutarch Solon). His own poems survive in fragments.
short_bio_en: Cancelled debts, ended debt slavery and tied political rights to wealth classes rather than birth; wrote poems defending his own moderation.

role_tag_en: reformer who founded Athenian democracy
dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 21 (Kenyon, MIT plain text, read 2026-10-11, this session): 'three years after the expulsion of the tyrants, in the archonship of Isagoras', Cleisthenes, now the popular leader, distributed the population into ten tribes and made the Council five hundred. With the expulsion in the archon year 511/510 (E_GR_012), that is 508/507, the range on E_GR_002. Herodotus 5.66.2 and 5.69.2 (Godley, read this session) tell the same reform without a year. No source read for this corpus gives his birth or his death, so both ranges are blank rather than filled from a conventional handbook date.
short_bio_en: Reorganised Athens into ten artificial tribes so that citizenship, not clan, defined political membership; the founding act of demokratia.

role_tag_en: Ionian philosopher of flux and logos
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.1 puts his floruit in the 69th Olympiad (504-501). Only fragments survive.
short_bio_en: Ephesian aristocrat who wrote that everything flows and that a single logos governs the cosmos.

role_tag_en: Athenian statesman; leader of the democracy 461-429
dating_basis: Death: Thucydides 2.65.6 (Crawley, MIT plain text, read 2026-10-11, this session): 'He outlived its commencement two years and six months', the commencement being the spring of 431 (2.2.1, read the same day), which places the death in 429, as on E_GR_030. Thucydides gives no cause of his death; the attribution to the plague is Plutarch's (Pericles 38), which was not read, so it is not made here. The birth range -495/-490 has no derivation recorded from any source read.
short_bio_en: Dominated Athenian politics for three decades; his funeral oration in Thucydides is the classic statement of democratic self-image.

role_tag_en: philosopher; put to death by the Athenian democracy
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 2.44 (Hicks; PerseusDL perseus-eng2, TEI section 2.5.44, read 2026-10-11, this session, with the Greek perseus-grc2 at the same section), citing Apollodorus's Chronology: he was born 'in the archonship of Apsephion, in the fourth year of the 77th Olympiad', and 'He died in the first year of the 95th Olympiad at the age of seventy', with which Demetrius of Phalerum agrees; 'some say he was sixty when he died'. On calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD, Ol. 95.1 = 400/399 BCE, so the death range is -400/-399. Ol. 77.4 = 469/468, and a death in 400/399 at seventy puts the birth in 470/469, so the birth range -470/-468 carries both readings rather than choosing. The 'sixty' of the unnamed others is recorded and not used, because Diogenes gives it against Apollodorus and Demetrius. Diogenes names no archon for the year of his death, and the name Laches occurs nowhere in book 2 of either file, so no archon is given here. Plato's Apology (Fowler; 24b-c and 37c-e read this session) is a contemporary witness to the trial (E_GR_005); no year is taken from it.
short_bio_en: Wrote nothing; questioned everyone; executed for impiety and corrupting the young. Western philosophy's founding martyr.

role_tag_en: philosopher; founder of the Academy
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 3.2-3 (Hicks; PerseusDL perseus-eng2, TEI sections 3.1.2-3, read 2026-10-11, this session). At 3.2: 'Apollodorus in his Chronology fixes the date of Plato's birth in the 88th Olympiad', and he died, according to Hermippus, 'in the first year of the 108th Olympiad, in his eightyfirst year'. At 3.3: 'Neanthes, however, makes him die at the age of eighty-four', and Plato was born in the archonship of Ameinias, 'the year of Pericles' death'. On calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD the 88th Olympiad is -428/-425 (the years in which its first and fourth years begin, the conversion used on P_ANAXAGORAS), and Ol. 108.1 = 348/347, which is the death range. Pericles' death is 429 in this corpus (E_GR_030, from Thucydides 2.65.6), and a death in 348/347 in his eighty-first year also puts the birth in 429/428; the birth range -429/-425 carries the Olympiad and that archon-year reading together rather than choosing. Neanthes's eighty-four, which would put the birth about 432, is recorded and not used, because Diogenes gives it as a dissent from Apollodorus and Hermippus.
short_bio_en: Socrates's student; his dialogues are the main source for Socrates and the origin of the theory of Forms.

role_tag_en: philosopher; founder of the Lyceum
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 5.9-10 (Hicks; PerseusDL perseus-eng2, TEI sections 5.1.9-10, read 2026-10-11, this session), citing Apollodorus's Chronology: 'he was born in the first year of the 99th Olympiad'; he 'retired to Chalcis in the third year of the 114th Olympiad and died a natural death, at the age of about sixty-three, in the archonship of Philocles'. On calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD, Ol. 99.1 = 384/383, which is the birth range. Ol. 114.3 = 322/321 is the earliest year for the death, and 'about sixty-three' from a birth in 384/383 reaches 321/320, so the death range is -322/-320. The archonship of Philocles is not converted here from the archon list.
short_bio_en: Plato's student for twenty years; systematised logic, ethics, politics and natural science.

role_tag_en: Milesian who explained the world without gods
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 1.37 (Hicks), citing Apollodorus's Chronology, places his birth in the first year of the 35th Olympiad (= 640/639 BCE on the conversion in calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD). DL 1.38 says he died in the 58th Olympiad (548-545) at seventy-eight, or ninety according to Sosicrates. The two statements do not agree: a birth in 640 and a life of seventy-eight years put his death in 562, while a death in 548-545 at seventy-eight puts his birth about 626. The birth range -640/-623 deliberately carries both readings rather than choosing. Herodotus 1.74.2 independently attests him foretelling the loss of daylight to the Ionians before the eclipse that stopped the Lydian-Median battle. The bio's place among the Seven Sages is DL 1.22 (read 2026-10-11, this session): 'As Plato testifies, he was one of the Seven Sages. He was the first to receive the name of Sage'.
short_bio_en: The first person in the Greek record to explain the world by something inside it rather than by the gods; he said everything came from water, foretold an eclipse, and was remembered as the first of the Seven Sages.

role_tag_en: Milesian who drew the first Greek map and wrote of the Boundless
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 2.2 (Hicks), citing Apollodorus's Chronology: Anaximander was sixty-four in the second year of the 58th Olympiad and 'died not long afterwards'. Ol. 58.2 = 547/546 BCE (calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD), which puts his birth in 611/610. The death range is left open to 540 because 'not long afterwards' is all the source says. Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy 3rd ed., in the chapter The Milesian School immediately before §13, observes that 547/6 is the year before the fall of Sardis and suggests Apollodorus found the indication in Anaximander's own book (read at en.wikisource.org 2026-09-08). The bio's quotation is Burnet's rendering in the same chapter, §13 (Q_027), re-read at en.wikisource.org 2026-10-11, this session.
short_bio_en: Thales's fellow-citizen, who made the first Greek map of the world and wrote that things arise from and return to the Boundless: 'they make reparation and satisfaction to one another for their injustice according to the ordering of time' — law-court language used of the cosmos.

role_tag_en: founder of a religious and political brotherhood in southern Italy
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 8.45 (Hicks) says only that he 'flourished in the 60th Olympiad' (= 540-537 BCE; calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD) and that his school lasted nine or ten generations. DL 8.3 has him leave Samos for Croton when he found his country under the tyranny of Polycrates. That floruit is recorded as the activity event E_GR_009. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date. A floruit is stored as a range on an event, never as a point on a person (conventions §2).
short_bio_en: Left Samos for Croton in southern Italy, where he and some three hundred followers governed the city and lived by rule; the tradition credits him with the transmigration of souls and with making number the key to the cosmos. Almost nothing about him is attested by a contemporary.

role_tag_en: wandering poet who attacked the gods people make in their own image
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.20 (Hicks) puts his floruit 'about the 60th Olympiad' (= 540-537 BCE); DL 9.18 says he was banished from Colophon and lived at Zancle and Catana. DL 9.19 quotes his own words that sixty-seven years had been tossing his cares up and down Greece, and that there were twenty-five more before that from his birth — a self-report of at least ninety-two years, which is a genuine constraint on his life but fixes no calendar year. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date.
short_bio_en: Said that if oxen and horses could paint they would paint gods like oxen and horses, and that Ethiopians make their gods snub-nosed and Thracians blue-eyed; also that the honour a city pays to athletes should go to wisdom instead.

role_tag_en: Eleatic poet-philosopher who argued that what is cannot not be
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.23 (Hicks): 'He flourished in the 69th Olympiad' (= 504-501 BCE; calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD) — the same Olympiad DL 9.1 gives for Heraclitus. DL 9.21 makes him a pupil of Xenophanes but a follower of the Pythagorean Ameinias, and DL 9.23 adds that he is said to have served his native city as a legislator. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date. r2-5 UPDATE (2026-09-09): the Parian Marble, permitted by L-30 and read this session, carries no entry for Parmenides, so the Marble does not unblock this row and both ranges stay blank. What this session could add is a scene, delivered as E_GR_042: Plato, Parmenides 127b (Fowler, PerseusDL, read at its locator this session) has Zeno and Parmenides come to Athens for the Great Panathenaea, Parmenides already quite elderly, about sixty-five years old, very white-haired, Zeno about forty, and Socrates then very young. That is a scene written by Plato two generations later and is NOT used to compute a birth year here; it is recorded as what a permitted source says, and the event row says the same thing in its summary.
short_bio_en: Wrote a hexameter poem in which a goddess shows him that only one road of inquiry can be followed — that it is — and that what can be thought and what can be are the same. Every later Greek account of being argues with him.

role_tag_en: Athenian tragic poet who put the Persian war on stage
dating_basis: DATED IN r2-5 FROM THE PARIAN MARBLE, which ruling L-30 admits and which was read at its locators this session in the 1788 Greek-Latin-English edition (SRC_PARIAN1788). Two entries do the work. Ep. 49: since the battle at Marathon was fought by the Athenians against the Persians, 227 years - and Aeschylus the poet was engaged in the action, being then 35 years of age. Ep. 60: since Aeschylus the poet, having lived 69 years, died at Gela in Sicily, 193 years. The two intervals are 34 years apart, so the stone itself puts his death 34 years after Marathon; Marathon is 490 in this corpus (E_GR_017, from Athenaion Politeia 22 and Herodotus 6.100-117), which gives a death about 456 and, with the stated 69 years, a birth about 525. Each range is widened by a year at each end because an age in whole years and an archon year straddling the Julian year cannot fix a single year, NOT to be tidy. The stone's own epoch archon-year is not used, because it was not established from the text read (see W_PARIAN). The earlier basis stands underneath: Herodotus 2.156.6 (Godley) attests Aeschylus son of Euphorion as an established poet by the time Herodotus wrote.
short_bio_en: Fought in the Persian wars: the Parian Marble has him in the battle at Marathon at thirty-five, and dying at Gela in Sicily at sixty-nine.

role_tag_en: the first historian; inquirer into why Greeks and Persians fought
dating_basis: Self-attested: the proem of the Histories (1.1) names the author of the inquiry. Internal references run down to about 430, which is the basis already recorded on W_HERODOTUS. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date. (Note on the text used: the proem of the PerseusDL Godley file reads 'Herodotus of Halicarnassus', re-read 2026-10-11, this session; the modern name Bodrum occurs there only inside the Perseus gazetteer annotation attached to the place name, which is markup and not the text.) r2-5 UPDATE (2026-09-09): the Parian Marble, permitted by L-30 and read this session, does NOT carry an entry for Herodotus - only the 1788 editor's dissertation discusses his dates, and those are the editor's, not the stone's, so nothing is taken from them. Birth and death therefore stay blank. What this session could add is a compositional window from the Histories themselves, and it is delivered as E_GR_043 rather than as a life range: 7.137 refers to the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians as something that has happened; 9.73 says the Lacedaemonians laid no hand on Decelea when they harried the rest of Attica, which is the annual invasions and not the later occupation; 6.98 names Darius, Xerxes and Artaxerxes as three generations of kings. All three read at their locators this session in the PerseusDL Godley file.
short_bio_en: Set out to preserve what men had done and to say why Greeks and Persians went to war, and in doing so recorded the customs of half the known world — including the observation that every nation believes its own customs the best.

role_tag_en: first and greatest of the sophists; teacher for a fee
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.56 (Hicks): 'according to some his death occurred, when he was on a journey, at nearly ninety years of age, though Apollodorus makes his age seventy, assigns forty years for his career as a sophist, and puts his floruit in the 84th Olympiad' (= 444-441 BCE; calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD). DL 9.50 has him born at Abdera and making laws for Thurii; DL 9.52 says the Athenians expelled him and burnt his books in the market-place. The sources disagree on his age by twenty years and give no calendar year for either end of his life, so both ranges are left blank rather than reconstructed.
short_bio_en: Opened his book Truth with 'man is the measure of all things' and his book On the Gods by saying he could not know whether they existed. Charged the first large fee for teaching and made arguing both sides of a question a discipline.

role_tag_en: put Mind above matter; tried at Athens for saying the sun is a stone
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 2.7 (Hicks), citing Apollodorus's Chronology: born in the 70th Olympiad (= 500-497 BCE) and died in the first year of the 88th Olympiad (= 428/427); conversion per calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD. DL adds in the same section that he was twenty at the invasion of Xerxes and lived seventy-two years, which agrees with those Olympiads to within a year or two — one of the few internally consistent chronologies in the Lives. DL 2.7 also puts his arrival at Athens in the archonship of Callias and gives him thirty years there. The bio's opening quotation is DL 2.6 (read 2026-10-11, this session), not 2.7.
short_bio_en: Opened his book 'All things were together; then came Mind and set them in order', and was prosecuted at Athens for saying that the sun was a mass of red-hot metal. Pericles was his pupil and, in one version, saved him.

role_tag_en: atomist: nothing exists but atoms and empty space
dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.34 (Hicks) says he met Leucippus and, according to some, Anaxagoras, 'being forty years younger than the latter'. Anaxagoras's birth is fixed by DL 2.7 to the 70th Olympiad (500-497), so forty years later gives 460-457. No permitted source read this session gives a death year — the usual c. 370 rests on later reports of his great age — so the death range is left blank.
short_bio_en: Held that the world is atoms moving in a void and that everything else — colour, sweetness, heat — exists only by convention.

role_tag_en: Athenian who spent the silver on ships and won Salamis
dating_basis: Near-contemporary and contemporary: Herodotus 7.144 credits him with persuading the Athenians to build ships with the Laurium silver, and books 8-9 with the strategy of Salamis; Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 22 dates that decision to the archonship of Nicodemus, and 23 makes him one of the two leaders of the people after the Persian wars. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date. A caution recorded openly: Ath. Pol. 25 also has him help Ephialtes against the Areopagus in the archonship of Conon, about 462/1, which cannot be reconciled with his exile; that chapter is the reason his later career is not given events in this batch. The bio rests on Herodotus 7.144.1-2 (Godley, read 2026-10-11, this session: the war 'saved Hellas by compelling the Athenians to become seamen') and Constitution of the Athenians 22 (Kenyon, read the same day: 'it was with these ships that they fought the battle of Salamis against the barbarians').
short_bio_en: Persuaded the Athenians to spend a windfall from the silver mines on warships instead of sharing it out. Herodotus says the war those ships were built for saved Greece by compelling the Athenians to become seamen; Aristotle's Constitution says they were the ships Athens fought with at Salamis.

role_tag_en: stripped the Areopagus and was murdered for it
dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 25 (Kenyon): the Areopagus was supreme 'for about seventeen years after the Persian wars', and then, 'in the archonship of Conon', Ephialtes stripped it of its acquired prerogatives; 'Not long afterwards, however, Ephialtes was assassinated by Aristodicus of Tanagra' (re-read 2026-10-11, this session, in the MIT plain text). Seventeen years from 479 gives about 462, and E_GR_024 carries the reform as -463/-461 for the word 'about' and the unconverted archon year; the death range begins with that reform range, at -463, and runs to -458 for the vagueness of 'not long afterwards'. No birth year is given anywhere, so that range is blank.
short_bio_en: Took the guardianship of the constitution away from the old aristocratic council and gave it to the Council of Five Hundred, the Assembly and the jury courts; he was killed within a few years and the change stood.

role_tag_en: comic poet whose Socrates walked on air
dating_basis: Plato, Apology 19c, has Socrates tell the jury that they saw the old slander for themselves 'in Aristophanes' comedy, a Socrates being carried about there, proclaiming that he was treading on air' — which attests Aristophanes as a known comic poet in Athens before 399 and his Clouds as a play the jurors had seen. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date. The usual dates (c. 446 - c. 386) and the production year of the Clouds rest on the ancient hypotheses and didascalic notices, which are not among the sources permitted for this batch; see open question 6. r2-5 UPDATE (2026-09-09): STILL UNDATED, and the reason is now specific rather than general. The Parian Marble, which L-30 admitted and which was read whole this session, carries no entry for Aristophanes; PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit holds no English text of the Clouds (the directory data/tlg0019/tlg002 contains only the Greek perseus-grc2 file, checked through the GitHub contents API this session), so the ancient hypothesis with its production year is not reachable by any permitted route tried today. The Apology 19c attestation recorded above therefore remains the whole of this row's dating, and it fixes only a terminus: the Clouds was a play the jurors of 399 had seen. This is the one Round-1 residue item that r2-5 could not close, and it is reported rather than filled. r3-5 UPDATE (2026-09-13), residue item 4: the production year of the Clouds is now reached by a permitted route and delivered as an event, E_GR_044 (423), from Hypothesis V in Starkie's 1911 edition (archive.org, public domain) with the archon year converted through Diodorus 12.65.1. Birth and death stay blank: nothing read this session gives either. CORRECTION to the r2-5 finding above: r2-5 checked PerseusDL data/tlg0019/tlg002, which is the Knights, not the Clouds. short_bio_en: Athenian comic poet; his caricature of Socrates as a sophist suspended in a basket was still being cited against Socrates a quarter of a century later, at his trial.

role_tag_en: brilliant, untrustworthy Athenian who changed sides twice
dating_basis: Contemporary: Thucydides names him repeatedly — 6.15 on his ambition for the Sicilian command, 6.53 and 6.61 on the Salaminia being sent to fetch him for trial, 6.61.6-7 and 6.88.9 on his escape from Thurii to the Peloponnese and to Lacedaemon (read 2026-10-11, this session), 8.45-56 on his intrigues at Samos and with Tissaphernes (book 8 beyond chapter 7 is read in the PerseusDL eng6 copy of Crawley, SRC_CRAWLEY_THUC_BK8, because the MIT text stops at 8.7; 8.45.1 and 8.56.2 re-read there the same day) — and Xenophon, Hellenica 1, on his return and second exile. Neither gives a birth or death year, and Thucydides' narrative breaks off in 411; both ranges are therefore left blank rather than taken from later biographies.
short_bio_en: Persuaded Athens into the Sicilian expedition, was recalled for sacrilege, defected to Sparta, then to Persia, then back to Athens.

role_tag_en: soldier who continued Thucydides and remembered Socrates
dating_basis: Self-attested as the author of the Hellenica, which takes up where Thucydides breaks off in 411 and runs to Mantinea in 362, and which at 3.1.2 refers to the march of Cyrus in 401 and the return of the Greeks as already narrated 'by Themistogenes the Syracusan'. That places him as an adult in 401 and alive after 362. No source among those permitted for this batch gives a birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from memory or from a conventional handbook date. The bio's march rests on Xenophon, Anabasis 3.1.4 and 3.1.47 (Brownson, PerseusDL perseus-eng2, read 2026-10-11, this session): 'There was a man in the army named Xenophon, an Athenian, who was neither general nor captain nor private', and after the generals were seized the army chose 'Xenophon the Athenian in place of Proxenus'. Hellenica 3.1.2, re-read the same day, attributes the account of the march to 'Themistogenes the Syracusan'; both are recorded and the attribution is not resolved here.
short_bio_en: Wrote the Hellenica, the history of his own times from where Thucydides breaks off. The Anabasis, the account of the march of the Ten Thousand into Persia and back, has an Athenian named Xenophon chosen general by the army; the Hellenica itself credits the account of that march to Themistogenes the Syracusan.

role_tag_en: tyrant of Miletus who abolished his own tyranny to raise a revolt
dating_basis: Herodotus 5.30-38, 5.49-51, 5.97-99 and 5.124-126 narrate his deputy-tyranny at Miletus, his failure at Naxos, his revolt, his embassies to Sparta and Athens, and his death in Thrace; 6.18 dates the fall of Miletus to the sixth year after his revolt. Herodotus gives no birth or death year, so both ranges are left blank.
short_bio_en: Deputy tyrant of Miletus who, having failed the Persians at Naxos, revolted, gave up his own tyranny to give Miletus equality under the law, deposed the other Ionian tyrants and drew Athens into the quarrel that led to Marathon.

role_tag_en: Athenian leader who argued that empire is a tyranny
dating_basis: Contemporary: Thucydides 3.36-40 gives him the speech for killing the Mytileneans and calls him at 3.36.6 'the most violent man at Athens'; 4.21-22 and 4.27-39 his Pylos command; 5.10 his death at Amphipolis. Diogenes Laertius 2.12 names a Cleon as the prosecutor of Anaxagoras. No birth or death year is stated in these sources — Thucydides dates events by summers and winters, not by persons — so both ranges are left blank.
short_bio_en: Argued openly that the empire was a tyranny that had to be feared to be kept, and that pity and clever speaking were luxuries an imperial city could not afford.

role_tag_en: chief minister of Zheng who published the law in bronze
dating_basis: Death: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 20 (= 522 BCE), which records his last illness, his advice to Zi Taishu that only a man of virtue can govern by leniency, and Confucius's reaction to the news — 出涕曰：「古之遺愛也。」, he wept and said 'a legacy of love from the ancients'. His government of Zheng begins at Zuozhuan, Xiang 30 (= 543), which describes his ordering of town and country. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Zhao 1 = 541 BCE). No birth year is given, so that range is blank. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. CHUNQIU RE-KEY: this person is also held by the chunqiu corpus as P_ZICHAN. short_bio_en: Ran the small state of Zheng between two great powers for twenty years and, in 536, had the penal code cast on a bronze vessel so that anyone could read it — the first published law in the Chinese record, and the first argument about whether law should be public.

role_tag_en: minister of Qi who saw his own ruling house dying
dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 3 (= 539 BCE) records his mission to Jin and his conversation with Shuxiang, in which he says of Qi 此季世也 — 'this is a last age' — and predicts that the state will pass to the Chen house; Zhao 20 and Zhao 26 record further advice to Duke Jing. No birth or death year is given in the Zuozhuan, so both ranges are blank. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. CHUNQIU RE-KEY: this person is also held by the chunqiu corpus as P_YANYING. short_bio_en: Served three rulers of Qi and told a foreign minister to his face that his own dynasty was finished, because the Chen family lent grain by the large measure and collected by the small. The prediction came true eight decades later.
map_place_basis: Display anchor: Linzi, the capital of the state he served (places.PL_LINZI carries polity_id POL_QI, which is this person's polity_id). The ruled class (L-95(2)): polity seat, one located event abroad, the capital emptied by a ruled override. POLITY SEAT: Qi is the state whose rulers he served, and Linzi is its capital. ONE LOCATED EVENT ABROAD: his only event link is E_CN_009 at Xintian (-539, present), Qi's envoy at the court of Jin, sent there in the Zuozhuan's own words 齊侯使晏嬰請繼室於晉 (Zhao 3, read this session at zh.wikisource.org, 春秋左氏傳/昭公, revision 10445713), so the computed rule (anchorOf() in site/engine/views/home_map.js: the located place of most `present` events, ties to the earliest) has one place to choose and draws Qi's minister under the name of Jin's capital, beside Shuxiang of Jin. No tie-break can fix that: with one located event there is no tie to break, and the deciding fact, that Qi is the state he served and Linzi its capital, is not in the event table the rule reads. What changed under it: E_CN_023 no longer sits at Linzi (its place is now PL_SHUZHOU, unlocated, ruling L-110(1)), so the 'capital emptied' paragraph above is history; Linzi keeps its pin through this override alone. role_tag_en: Jin grandee who argued that law should not be published
dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 6 (= 536 BCE) preserves his letter to Zichan against casting the penal code; Zhao 3 (= 539) his conversation with Yan Ying, in which he says the Jin ducal house is equally in its last age; Zhao 28 records the destruction of his clan. No birth or death year is given, so both ranges are blank. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. wikidata_qid Q831231: the item is a human labelled 叔向 with no English description, but its Japanese sitelink and Chinese alias are 羊舌肸 and its occupation is politician — checked at wikidata.org 2026-09-08, which is why it is recorded rather than left blank. short_bio_en: Wrote the classic argument against publishing law: once people know the exact rules they will argue from the text instead of deferring to their betters, and litigation and bribery will multiply. He lost, and every later Chinese state published its law.

The capital-of-the-state-served family (ruled L-112, 2026-10-04: the fifth member after P_DUKE_AI_LU, P_FUCHAI, P_WUZIXU and P_YANYING). So, unlike P_YANYING's case, an event does record him at the drawn place: the override's evidence tier is 'present', and the stated-only card sentence correctly does not fire. Ruled L-110(3)/L-112; executed Sophia r9-1.
map_place_reason: Shuxiang was a grandee of Jin, and Xintian had been Jin's capital since 585 BCE. The Zuozhuan records him at the Jin court in 539 BCE, receiving Qi's envoy Yan Ying. He went to Song once, in 546 BCE, as deputy to Jin's delegate at the peace conference; a count of events would draw him there, so the atlas draws him in the state he served instead.

role_tag_en: general credited with the Art of War; existence disputed
dating_basis: Shiji 65 (Biographies of Sun Zi and Wu Qi), read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08, opens 孫子武者，齊人也。以兵法見於吳王闔廬 — 'Master Sun, named Wu, was a man of Qi; he gained an audience with King Helü of Wu on the strength of his art of war' — and ends by crediting him with the westward breaking of Chu and the entry into Ying (506). AGAINST that: the Zuozhuan, which narrates the Wu-Chu war of 506 in detail (Ding 4), never mentions him. historicity is therefore 'traditional', not 'attested': the tradition assigns him a place and a period, but the near-contemporary narrative of the campaign he is credited with does not know his name. No source gives birth or death years; both ranges are blank.
short_bio_en: The name attached to the Art of War. Sima Qian tells how he drilled the king's concubines and beheaded two of them to prove that a general in the field need not obey even his ruler; the annals of the war he supposedly won do not mention him.

role_tag_en: exile from Chu who made Wu strong and was made to kill himself
dating_basis: Death: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 11 (= 484 BCE) — he warns Fuchai that Yue is a disease of the heart and belly, is not listened to, is sent on an embassy to Qi, and on his return the king 'sent him the Zhulou sword that he might die' (使賜之屬鏤以死); his dying words are that Wu will perish. Zuozhuan, Ding 4 (= 506) already has him as Wu's envoy plotting against Chu (伍員為吳行人以謀楚). No birth year is given, so that range is blank. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. CHUNQIU RE-KEY: this person is also held by the chunqiu corpus as P_WUYUAN — an id that DIFFERS from this project's P_WUZIXU (chunqiu uses the form 伍员). short_bio_en: Fled Chu after his family was killed, spent his life turning Wu into the power that destroyed Chu, and was ordered to kill himself for saying that Wu's real enemy was the neighbour it had spared. He was right within eleven years.
map_place_basis: Display anchor: Gusu, the capital of the state he served (places.PL_GUSU carries polity_id POL_WU, which is this person's polity_id) and the place where he was made to kill himself (E_CN_019, -484). Recomputed from data/csv/ this session, 2026-09-25: the computed rule (anchorOf() — most `present` events, ties to the earliest) counts three located `present` places at one each — E_CN_013 at Ying (-506), E_CN_018 at Kuaiji (-494), E_CN_019 at Gusu (-484) — and breaks the three-way tie to the earliest, anchoring the exile from Chu at Chu's own capital, which he entered once, at the head of an invading army, twenty-two years before he died there in Wu. A tie-break cannot fix that: the deciding fact, that Wu is the state he served and Gusu its capital, is not in the event table. Ruled L-84(1)/L-87(4); Vision r5-6 §8(1). map_place_reason: Wu Zixu fled Chu after his father and brother were killed, and served the kings of Wu for the rest of his life; Gusu is the conventional name for Wu's capital. A count of events would draw him at Ying, the Chu capital Wu's army took in 506 BCE. The atlas draws him in the state he served, where he was ordered to kill himself in 484 BCE.

role_tag_en: adviser who rebuilt Yue and then walked away from the reward
dating_basis: Shiji 41 (Hereditary House of King Goujian of Yue), read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 范蠡事越王句踐 — he served Goujian, shared twenty years of deep planning with him, destroyed Wu and wiped out the shame of Kuaiji, was named supreme general, and then left by sea and never returned, warning his colleague Wen Zhong that when the flying birds are finished the good bow is put away (蜚鳥盡，良弓藏). historicity is 'probable' rather than 'attested': the Zuozhuan years covering the Wu-Yue war (Ding 14, Ai 1, Ai 22) name Wen Zhong but were searched this session and do not name Fan Li, so he rests on Sima Qian four centuries later. No birth or death year is given anywhere; both ranges are blank.
short_bio_en: Goujian's strategist through twenty years of humiliation and revenge, and the first figure in the Chinese record to leave power voluntarily at the moment of victory, on the argument that a ruler who shares hardship will not share ease.

role_tag_en: disciple of Confucius who made filial duty the centre
dating_basis: Shiji 67 (Biographies of the Disciples of Confucius), read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 曾參，南武城人，字子輿。少孔子四十六歲 — 'Zeng Shen, a man of Nan Wucheng, styled Ziyu; forty-six years younger than Confucius'. Confucius's birth is fixed by E_CN_001 to -552/-551, so Zengzi's birth falls in -506/-505. No death year is given in that chapter, so the death range is blank. (Wikidata Q1207671 gives 505-435 BCE; the 435 is not carried here because no permitted source supports it.)
short_bio_en: One of the youngest disciples and the one the later tradition made its moral anchor: the Analects has him examine himself on three points every day, and the classic of filial duty was written in his name.

role_tag_en: disciple who became a teacher of rulers in Wei
dating_basis: Shiji 67 (Biographies of the Disciples of Confucius), read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 卜商字子夏。少孔子四十四歲 — 'Bu Shang, styled Zixia; forty-four years younger than Confucius'. With Confucius's birth at -552/-551 (E_CN_001) that gives -508/-507. No death year is given, so that range is blank. His later teaching at Xihe under Marquis Wen of Wei is reported by Shiji 67 as well, but without a year.
short_bio_en: The disciple most associated with transmitting the classics; the tradition makes him the teacher of the rulers and ministers of Wei, and so the channel by which the Confucian texts reached the Warring States courts.

role_tag_en: preached impartial care and defended cities against attack
dating_basis: Shiji 74, the closing notice of the Biographies of Mencius and Xun Qing, read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08, is the whole of what the early record says: 墨翟，宋之大夫，善守御，為節用。或曰并孔子時，或曰在其後 — 'Mo Di, a grandee of Song, skilled in defence, advocated frugality. Some say he was contemporary with Confucius, some say he came after him.' Sima Qian himself records the disagreement and does not resolve it, so no birth or death range is entered here. The school's activity is carried by the activity event E_CN_031 instead.
short_bio_en: Argued that the world's disorder comes from people loving their own family, house and state and not others', and that the cure is to care for everyone alike; his followers were also the best military engineers of their day, hired to defend cities against the sieges he condemned.

role_tag_en: ruler of Lu in Confucius's last years
dating_basis: Reign: the Zuozhuan's Duke Ai section runs from Ai 1 to Ai 27, which is -494 to -468 on the Lu ducal conversion in calendars.csv CAL_LU; the Chunqiu classic ends in his fourteenth year with the capture of the lin. He appears in the Analects (2.19, 3.21, 6.3, 12.9) asking Confucius about government. No birth or death year is given in these sources; both ranges are blank, and the reign is carried by events rather than by a life range.
short_bio_en: The duke under whom Confucius came home to Lu and died; the Zuozhuan gives him the lament over Confucius's grave, and the Analects gives him the questions of a ruler who cannot control his own great families.

name_alt: King Helü of Wu; 闔廬
role_tag_en: king of Wu who broke Chu and died of a toe wound
dating_basis: Death: Zuozhuan, Duke Ding year 14 (= 496 BCE) — at Zuili, Goujian's condemned men cut their own throats in front of the Wu line, Yue attacked in the confusion, Linggufu struck Helü with a dagger-axe and took off his big toe, and he died at Xing, seven li from Zuili (闔廬傷將指…還卒於陘). His victory over Chu is at Ding 4 (= 506). No birth year is given, so that range is blank. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. short_bio_en: Took Wu from a southern outsider to the power that entered the Chu capital in 506; five years of hard living and shared rations, the Zuozhuan says, were why his men fought. Killed by a wound to the foot in a battle with Yue.

role_tag_en: king of Wu who spared Yue and lost his kingdom to it
dating_basis: Death: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 22 (= 473 BCE) — 'in winter, in the eleventh month, on the day dingmao, Yue extinguished Wu' and offered the king a residence at Yongdong; he refused, saying 'I am old, how can I serve a lord?', and hanged himself (乃縊). His victory at Fujiao is at Ai 1 (= 494) and his contest for the hegemony at Huangchi at Ai 13 (= 482). No birth year is given. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. CHUNQIU RE-KEY: this person is also held by the chunqiu corpus as P_FUCHA — an id that DIFFERS from this project's P_FUCHAI. short_bio_en: Beat Yue in 494 and let it live, against Wu Zixu's advice; spent twenty years fighting for primacy in the north while Goujian rebuilt behind him, and hanged himself when Yue finally took his capital.

The king of Wu belongs under Wu's capital, not under the mountain of the enemy state he spared. Recomputed from data/csv/ this session, 2026-09-25: of his five event links two name no place (E_CN_020, E_CN_022) and one counts only as `related` (E_CN_019 at Gusu), so the computed rule (anchorOf() — most `present` events, ties to the earliest) sees a one-to-one tie, E_CN_018 at Kuaiji (-494) against E_CN_025 at Gusu (-473), and breaks it to the earlier, drawing him at Yue's stronghold among Yue's people. A tie-break cannot fix that either: the deciding fact, that Gusu is his own capital, is not in the event table. Ruled L-84(1)/L-87(4); Vision r5-6 §8(1). role_tag_en: king of Yue who lost, submitted, waited and destroyed Wu

No birth or death year is given in the Zuozhuan, so both ranges are blank; Wikidata Q1267918 gives a reign 496-465, which is not carried here because no permitted source read this session supports it. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU. Read at ctext.org 2026-09-08. CHUNQIU RE-KEY: this person is also held by the chunqiu corpus as P_GOUJIAN. Map read from chunqiu's data/csv/people.csv by the lead, 2026-09-08, ruling L-34; the chunqiu repository was not opened from this session. people.csv has no note column, so this provenance lives here; a note column is a Round-2 schema candidate.
short_bio_en: Beaten and made to submit in 494, he spent twenty years cultivating his people and his patience and then destroyed the kingdom that had spared him — the model of endurance in the Chinese political imagination ever since.

role_tag_en: disciple of Confucius who commanded Lu's left wing
dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 11 (= 484 BCE) makes him steward of the Ji family, argues the Ji head into fighting the Qi invasion, and gives him the command of the left wing with three hundred men of Wucheng as his own troops; the Analects (6.12, 11.17, 16.1) has Confucius criticise him for enriching the Ji family. No birth or death year is given in these sources, so both ranges are blank; Wikidata Q840352 gives a birth of 522, which is not carried here for want of a permitted source. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU.
short_bio_en: The disciple who actually held power: as the Ji family's steward he won the battle that brought Confucius home from exile, and was rebuked by his teacher for collecting taxes for a house already too rich.

role_tag_en: king of Babylon who took Jerusalem and deported Judah
dating_basis: Regnal years, not a life. Read this session: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 Rev. 11-13 dates the capture of Jerusalem to the second day of Addaru in his seventh year; 2 Kings 25:8 dates the burning of the Temple to the fifth month of his nineteenth year; Jeremiah 32:1 equates the tenth year of Zedekiah with his eighteenth; Jeremiah 52:28-30 counts deportations in his seventh, eighteenth and twenty-third years. BIRTH: no source read gives one, so both birth cells are blank. DEATH: inferred, and the inference is stated rather than hidden - 2 Kings 25:27 puts the release of Jehoiachin in the thirty-seventh year of that captivity and in the accession year of Evil-merodach, which places the end of Nebuchadnezzar's reign in the same year; counting the captivity from the deportation of 597 gives 562/561, and the two-year range carries the Nisan-year straddle. This is a derived date, not one any source read this session states.
short_bio_en: The Babylonian king whose armies twice broke Jerusalem, deported its ruling class and burned its Temple. In the biblical books he is the instrument of a judgement and hardly a character; in his own chronicles he is a king on campaign in the Hatti-land, appointing a king of his own choice and receiving heavy tribute.

role_tag_en: last king of Judah, installed by Babylon and blinded by it
dating_basis: 2 Kings 24:17-18, read this session: Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's father's brother, king in his stead and changed his name to Zedekiah; he was twenty-one years old when he began to reign and reigned eleven years. His accession is the deportation of 597 (ABC 5 Rev. 11-13), so he was born about 619-617; the three-year range carries the accession-year and Nisan-year slack. DEATH: no source read gives a year. 2 Kings 25:7 has his sons killed before his eyes, his own eyes put out and himself carried to Babylon in fetters, and then says nothing further, so both death cells are blank.
short_bio_en: Put on the throne of Judah by the king who had just carried off his nephew, and destroyed by rebelling against him. He is the king through whose eleven years Jeremiah argues and Ezekiel prophesies from exile, and the last king Judah had.

role_tag_en: king of Judah deported in 597; the exile is dated by his captivity
dating_basis: 2 Kings 24:8, read this session: eighteen years old at his accession, and he reigned three months. His accession and deportation are fixed by ABC 5 Rev. 11-13 (second of Addaru, seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar = February/March 597), so he was born about 617-615. DEATH: no source read gives a year; 2 Kings 25:27-30 has him lifted out of prison in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity and then eating bread before the king of Babylon continually, with a daily allowance, 'all the days of his life' (25:29-30); the verses give no year for the end of that life, so the death cells are blank rather than guessed. 2 Kings 25:27-30 read at its locator on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version. This person matters chronologically out of proportion to his three months on the throne: Ezekiel dates his own oracles by the years of this man's captivity (Ezekiel 1:2).
short_bio_en: King of Judah for three months, then a prisoner in Babylon for thirty-seven years, then a man eating at the Babylonian king's table. The exile counted its years from his deportation, which is why a boy king who did nothing became the calendar of a century.

role_tag_en: prophet who told Judah to surrender and to build in exile
dating_basis: Neither birth nor death is given by anything read this session, so both ranges are blank. His dated activity, read this session: Jeremiah 25:1 sets an oracle in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, which the verse itself equates with the first year of Nebuchadnezzar; Jeremiah 32:1-2 sets the purchase of the field in the tenth year of Zedekiah, the eighteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, while the army was besieging Jerusalem and he was shut up in the court of the guard; Jeremiah 39-41 has him in the land after the fall, with Gedaliah at Mizpah. The person is known from the book that bears his name, which is why historicity is probable and not attested.
short_bio_en: The prophet who told his city that resistance was a lie and that the exiles should build houses in Babylon and pray for the peace of the city that had taken them. He bought a field in a village under enemy occupation as a sign that there would be a later.

role_tag_en: Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, murdered at Mizpah
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Position and end, read this session: 2 Kings 25:22 has Nebuchadnezzar make Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, governor over the people left in the land; 2 Kings 25:25 and Jeremiah 41:1-2 both put his murder in the seventh month, without a year.
short_bio_en: The man Babylon left in charge of what was left of Judah. He was killed at dinner in the seventh month by a member of the royal family, and the survivors fled to Egypt rather than wait for the reprisal.

role_tag_en: prince of the royal house who killed Gedaliah
dating_basis: No dates in anything read this session; both ranges blank. He is placed only by the act: 2 Kings 25:25 and Jeremiah 41:1-2, read this session, name him as of the seed royal and one of the chief officers of the king, and put the killing in the seventh month.
short_bio_en: A survivor of the royal line who ate bread with the governor at Mizpah and then killed him with ten men - the last act of the Judahite monarchy, and the one that emptied the land.

role_tag_en: king of Babylon who released Jehoiachin from prison
dating_basis: 2 Kings 25:27, read this session, dates his accession year to the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, which counting from 597 is 562/561. Neither birth nor death is given by anything read this session, so both ranges are blank; only the accession is anchored, and it is anchored on E_IL_018.
short_bio_en: Nebuchadnezzar's successor, remembered in the Hebrew Bible for one act: he brought the captive king of Judah out of prison, spoke kindly to him and set his seat above the other captive kings. The Book of Kings ends on that sentence.

role_tag_en: last king of Babylon, absent at Tayma when Cyrus came
dating_basis: Regnal years only. The Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7), re-read at livius.org this session, dates by his regnal years - the seventh year has the king in Tayma while the prince, his officers and his army were in Akkad, and the Akitu festival did not take place - and its column III carries the fall of Babylon already recorded on E_PE_001. No birth or death year is given by anything read this session, so both ranges are blank.
short_bio_en: The king who was not in his own capital. His chronicle records year after year in which he stayed at Tayma in Arabia and the new-year festival could not be held, and then the year Cyrus walked into Babylon.

role_tag_en: prince of Judah who carried the Temple vessels home
dating_basis: No dates in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Position: Ezra 1:8 and 1:11, read this session, call him the prince of Judah, have Cyrus's treasurer Mithredath count the vessels out to him, and say he brought them up from Babylon to Jerusalem when the captivity was brought up - which places him in or after the first year of Cyrus over Babylon (E_IL_004, 538).
short_bio_en: The man Ezra names as receiving five thousand four hundred gold and silver vessels from the Persian treasury and bringing them back to Jerusalem. The book never explains how he relates to Zerubbabel, who does the building.

role_tag_en: governor of Judah under Darius who rebuilt the Temple
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Dated activity: Haggai 1:1, read this session, addresses him as Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, in the second year of Darius the king, sixth month, first day; Haggai 1:14 has him start work on the twenty-fourth day of that month; Ezra 3:8 has him begin the oversight of the house in the second month of the second year of the return.
short_bio_en: The Davidic governor under whom the Second Temple was actually built. Two prophets stood at his elbow telling him to get on with it, and the book that records the finished building gives him no crown.

role_tag_en: high priest of the returned community
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Dated activity: Haggai 1:1 and 1:14 name him as the high priest beside Zerubbabel in the second year of Darius; Ezra 3:8 has him beside Zerubbabel at the start of the work. Ezra spells the name Jeshua son of Jozadak and Haggai spells it Joshua son of Jehozadak; name_alt carries both, as read this session.
short_bio_en: The priest half of the pair that rebuilt the Temple. After the monarchy ended, the high priest is the office that carries the community, and this is where that begins to be visible in the record.

role_tag_en: prophet who shamed the returnees into rebuilding the Temple
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Every one of his oracles is stamped, and all four stamps fall in the second year of Darius: Haggai 1:1 (sixth month, first day), 1:15 (sixth month, twenty-fourth day), 2:1 (seventh month, twenty-first day), 2:10 and 2:20 (ninth month, twenty-fourth day) - all read this session. Darius's second year is 520/519, counting from the accession established on E_PE_002.
short_bio_en: A prophet with a single argument and four dated speeches: you live in panelled houses while the house of God lies waste. Three weeks after the first speech the building started.

role_tag_en: prophet of the rebuilding, who saw the future in night visions
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Three date stamps, read this session: Zechariah 1:1 (eighth month, second year of Darius), 1:7 (twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, second year) and 7:1 (fourth day of the ninth month, Chislev, fourth year). Ezra 6:14 pairs him with Haggai as the two prophets through whose prophesying the elders built.
short_bio_en: The other prophet of the rebuilding, and a stranger one: his oracles come as a sequence of night visions with an interpreting angel, a form that outlives him by centuries.

role_tag_en: priest and scribe who brought the Law from Babylon and read it out
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Dated activity, read this session: Ezra 7:7-9 puts his going up in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, leaving Babylon on the first day of the first month and reaching Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth; Nehemiah 8:2-3 has him read the Law on the first day of the seventh month. WHICH Artaxerxes the book means is not stated by it and is a standing dispute; E_IL_030 carries the resulting range and the disclosure about the Julian conversion.
short_bio_en: A priest who is introduced not by his altar but by his reading: a ready scribe in the Law of Moses, who had set his heart to seek it, to do it, and to teach it. After him the community is organised around a book.

role_tag_en: Persian cupbearer who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem
dating_basis: No birth or death year in anything read this session; both ranges blank. Dated activity, read this session: Nehemiah 1:1 puts him in Shushan the castle in the month Chislev of the twentieth year, and 2:1 has him before the king in the month Nisan in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king. The same Artaxerxes ambiguity as for Ezra applies; see E_IL_032. The bio's opposition, read at its locators on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version: Nehemiah 2:10 and 2:19 (Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arabian are grieved, laugh the builders to scorn and ask whether they will rebel against the king), 4:1-2 (they and the Arabians, the Ammonites and the Ashdodites conspire to come and fight against Jerusalem; JPS 1917 numbers chapter 4 as the Hebrew does, so these are 4:7-8 in Bibles that end chapter 3 at verse 32) and 6:1-14 (the invitations to Ono, the open letter, the hired prophet).
short_bio_en: The one figure of the Persian period who tells his own story in the first person. He was a cupbearer at Susa, asked for leave, and rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem while Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem and their allies mocked him, plotted against him and threatened to attack.

role_tag_en: Persian king in whose reign Ezra and Nehemiah are dated
dating_basis: r3-5 (2026-09-13): dated from a chronology read at its locator (residue item 6). Parker & Dubberstein, Babylonian Chronology (1942), pp. 15-16 (SRC_PD1942, read this session): Xerxes dead and Artaxerxes acceded before the end of 465 (Elephantine papyrus of 3 January 464, 'year 21, the accession year of Artaxerxes'); his year 1 under way by June 464; last tablets of his year 41 in December 424, possibly February 423; Darius II king by 13 February 423. Death therefore -424/-423. Birth is not attested; blank. The earlier basis stands underneath and agrees: Thucydides 4.50.3 (read 2026-09-09 in the MIT Crawley text and again 2026-09-13 in the PerseusDL Crawley and Hobbes files) reports the death of King Artaxerxes son of Xerxes in the winter that ends the war's seventh year, 425/424 on Thucydides's count; 1.137.3 has Themistocles write to him as newly come to the throne; Herodotus 6.98 names Darius, Xerxes and Artaxerxes as three generations. Diodorus 11.69 (read this session) tells his accession in the archonship of Lysitheus, 465/464. wikidata_qid Q189689: 'Artaxerxes I', 'sixth Achaemenid emperor (475–424 BC)' (read 2026-10-13 through the wikidata.org API; en.wikipedia's article 'Artaxerxes I' names the same item as its wikibase_item, read the same day). Until 2026-10-13 this row carried Q170318, which is the item 'M16 rifle' ('rifle'), read the same day.
short_bio_en: The Persian king whose regnal years date the reorganisation of Judah under Ezra and Nehemiah - if he is the Artaxerxes those books mean, which they never say.

role_tag_en: king of Magadha and the order's first royal patron
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. The absolute frame is P_BUDDHA's, which follows Bechert's short chronology (death c. 400 plus or minus twenty). Relative order read this session: pli-tv-kd1:22.1-22.18 has King Seniya Bimbisara of Magadha give the Bamboo Grove to the order soon after the awakening; pli-tv-kd17:3.4-3.5 has Devadatta tell Prince Ajatasattu to kill his father and become king, and dn2:99.6 has Ajatasattu, now king, confess to the Buddha that he took the life of his father, a just and principled king. So Bimbisara's death falls inside the Buddha's teaching life and before DN 2 and DN 16, in which Ajatasattu reigns.
short_bio_en: The Magadhan king who gave the new order its first piece of property, a bamboo park outside his capital, and was later killed by his own son. Magadha is the state that will swallow northern India, and this is the reign in which it starts.

role_tag_en: king of Magadha who killed his father and attacked the Vajjis
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. The absolute frame is P_BUDDHA's, which follows Bechert's short chronology (death c. 400 plus or minus twenty). Relative order read this session: he is a prince under Devadatta's influence at pli-tv-kd17:2.1 and 3.4; he is king and confesses the killing at dn2:99.6-102.4; he is king and planning to destroy the Vajjis in the opening lines of DN 16 (1.1.3), which is the last year of the Buddha's life; and he claims a share of the relics after the death (dn16:6.24.1-4). His reign therefore overlaps the end of the Buddha's life on the canon's own account, and this batch dates nothing of his by a calendar year.
short_bio_en: Killed his father for the throne, asked the Buddha what good renunciation does, and was told at length; sent a minister to ask whether he could destroy the Vajjian republic, and was answered with a description of what keeps a republic from falling.

role_tag_en: king of Kosala, the Buddha's other royal patron
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. The absolute frame is P_BUDDHA's, which follows Bechert's short chronology (death c. 400 plus or minus twenty). Placed by his kingdom rather than by a year: Kosala is Magadha's northern rival, and the discourses set at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove (MN 135:1.2, read this session) are in his capital. No text read this session dates any event of his reign. A passage that names him, read at its locator on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in suttacentral/bilara-data, published branch, Sujato's translation: SN 3.1, where King Pasenadi of Kosala comes to the Buddha in Jeta's Grove near Savatthi (sn3.1:1.2-1.3), asks why one 'so young in age and newly gone forth' claims an awakening the six founders do not claim (2.1-2.4), and goes for refuge as a lay follower (14.1-14.5). It dates nothing.
short_bio_en: King of Kosala in the Buddha's lifetime. In one discourse, set in Jeta's Grove near Savatthi, he asks how so young a teacher can claim an awakening the six famous founders do not claim, and ends by going for refuge as a lay follower.

role_tag_en: the Buddha's chief disciple, the analyst of the teaching
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. Relative order read this session: pli-tv-kd1:23-24.7 gives the going forth of Sariputta and Moggallana, who come over with two hundred and fifty of Sanjaya's wanderers (kd1:24.5.3); dn16:1.16 has him make his lion's roar before the Buddha at Nalanda during the last journey. The tradition that he predeceased the Buddha was not verified in this session and is not recorded.
short_bio_en: The disciple the tradition made its analyst: where the Buddha says a thing briefly, Sariputta is the one asked to say it in detail. He came into the order out of a rival school, bringing most of it with him.

role_tag_en: the Buddha's second chief disciple, the meditator
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. The absolute frame is P_BUDDHA's, which follows Bechert's short chronology (death c. 400 plus or minus twenty). Relative order read this session: he goes forth together with Sariputta out of Sanjaya's school (pli-tv-kd1:23-24.7). No text read this session dates anything of his by a year. Re-read for the bio at pli-tv-kd1:23.1.1-24.7.4 on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in suttacentral/bilara-data, published branch, Brahmali's translation.
short_bio_en: Sariputta's companion from before either of them met the Buddha: the two left Sanjaya's school together and took its wanderers with them to the Buddha.

role_tag_en: the Buddha's attendant, who is present at almost everything
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. He is the constant companion of the last journey: he is standing behind the Buddha fanning him in the opening scene (dn16:1.4.1), is told to live as his own island (dn16:2.26.1), sets up the cot between the sal trees (dn16:5.1.5), and announces the death to the Mallas (dn16:6.12). All read this session; none of it carries a year. The bio's recitation, read at its locator on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in suttacentral/bilara-data, published branch, Brahmali's translation: Mahākassapa asks Ānanda about the Teaching (pli-tv-kd21:1.8.1-1.8.17), 'In this way he asked about the five collections. Ānanda was able to reply to each and every question' (1.8.18-19). The opening formula 'So I have heard' read the same day at dn2:1.1, dn29:1.1 and sn3.1:1.1.
short_bio_en: The attendant who was there. At the first communal recitation, by the monastic law's account, he was the one questioned on the teaching, and he answered for all five collections; each discourse opens with the words 'So I have heard.'

role_tag_en: senior monk who convened the council after the Buddha died
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. Relative order read this session: dn16:6.19-6.22 has him arrive at Kusinara after the death and approach the pyre; pli-tv-kd21:1.1.2-1.1.10 has him on the road from Pava to Kusinara hear from an Ajivaka that it is seven days since the Buddha attained final extinguishment, and it is he who then proposes the recitation.
short_bio_en: The monk who heard of the Buddha's death from a passer-by carrying a flower, and who, hearing an old monk say it was a relief to be free of the teacher, decided the teaching had better be recited and fixed before anyone forgot it.

role_tag_en: monk who told the others when the Buddha had actually died
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. The absolute frame is P_BUDDHA's, which follows Bechert's short chronology (death c. 400 plus or minus twenty). Placed by dn16:6.8.2-6.11.14 and 6.14.5-6.15.6, read this session: he tells Ananda that the Buddha has entered the cessation of perception and feeling and is not yet extinguished, and afterwards explains to the Mallas why the corpse cannot be lifted.
short_bio_en: The one person in the room who could tell the difference between a deep meditative state and death, and said so.

role_tag_en: monk who tried to split the order and to have the Buddha killed
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. The Pali canon dates nothing by a calendar year; it gives only relative order, and the relative order this batch could read is recorded here. The absolute frame is P_BUDDHA's, which follows Bechert's short chronology (death c. 400 plus or minus twenty). Placed by pli-tv-kd17:2.1-3.6, read this session: he wins Prince Ajatasattu with a display of power, is warned about by the Buddha, then tells the prince to kill his father while he kills the Buddha, and sends men to do it. All of this falls inside the Buddha's teaching life and before Bimbisara's death. Kinship and the chapter, read at their locators on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in suttacentral/bilara-data, published branch, Brahmali's translation and the Mahāsaṅgīti root: the chapter opens with the young Sakyans who follow the Buddha into homelessness, Devadatta among them with Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Ānanda and Bhagu and Kimila (pli-tv-kd17:1.1.2, 1.4.1, 1.4.30); no segment read calls him the Buddha's cousin, so the bio does not. The chapter's title is 'The chapter on schism in the Sangha' (pli-tv-kd17:0.3, Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka), which does not name him.
short_bio_en: A Sakyan who went forth with Ananda and Anuruddha, then wanted the order for himself and made an alliance with a prince who wanted his father's throne. The monastic law tells his story in its chapter on schism in the Sangha.

role_tag_en: chief minister of Magadha who came to ask about the Vajjis
dating_basis: NO SOURCE READ IN THIS SESSION GIVES THIS PERSON A BIRTH OR A DEATH YEAR, so both ranges are left blank rather than filled from a handbook. Placed by dn16:1.2.1-1.3.7 (he is sent to the Vulture's Peak to report the king's intention) and dn16:1.26.1-1.29.4 (he and Sunidha are building the fortress at Pataligama), both read this session, and both inside the last year of the Buddha's life.
short_bio_en: The brahmin minister sent to find out whether Magadha could destroy the Vajjian league, and one of the two chief ministers building a citadel at Pataligama to keep the Vajjis out.

role_tag_en: courtesan of Vesali who gave her mango grove to the order

short_bio_en: A courtesan who beat the aristocracy of her city to an invitation and would not sell it back at any price, and who ended by giving away the park she had entertained in.

short_bio_en: The teacher whose school Sariputta and Moggallana left; by the monastic law's account they took all two hundred and fifty of his wanderers with them. The canon reports his answer to every question as a refusal either to affirm or to deny.

short_bio_en: Chief minister of Qi in the seventh century BCE, credited with making Duke Huan the first leader of the feudal lords. He enters this atlas through Confucius's argument about him a century and a half later: Guan Zhong broke the loyalty code by serving his lord's killer, and yet, Confucius says, he united the states without war chariots, and without him 'we would be wearing our hair loose and our robes fastened on the left'. The book that bears his name was written by others.

role_tag_en: blind music master of Jin who said rulers exist for the people
dating_basis: No birth or death year is given; both ranges are blank. The row is held by one reported speech: Zuozhuan, 襄公十四年 傳 (= -559), read at zh.wikisource.org page 春秋左氏傳/襄公 (revision 9172568, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session): 師曠侍於晉侯 — he answers the marquis of Jin's question about the people of Wei driving out their ruler (Q_113). short_bio_en: The music master at the court of Jin. When the people of Wei drove out their ruler in 559 BCE and the marquis of Jin asked whether that was not going too far, Shi Kuang answered that a ruler who ruins the people is of no use, that Heaven set up rulers to shepherd the people, and that Heaven would never let one man run riot over them. It is the earliest statement in this atlas that the people, not the ruler, are the point of government.

short_bio_en: A minister of the state of Song, a middle-sized state caught between the two great powers of Jin and Chu. He was on good terms with leaders on both sides and in 579 BCE brought them to swear a written covenant outside Song's west gate: neither would make war on the other. It did not last, but it was the first such treaty in the record.

short_bio_en: A minister of Song who, in 546 BCE, persuaded Jin, Chu and the other states to send delegates to Song and swear to stop the wars among the feudal lords. The chronicle says plainly that he wanted the credit, and afterwards asked to be rewarded with towns; a colleague told him that no one can abolish arms and had his grant cancelled.

dating_basis: Death: Zuozhuan, 定公九年 傳 (= -501), read at zh.wikisource.org page 春秋左氏傳/定公 (revision 2371915, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session): 鄭駟歂殺鄧析．而用其竹刑 (E_CN_042, Q_112).
